headline: The Federal Reserve held rates but two officials voted to hike, and chair Kevin Warsh's patient tone pulled the dollar off a two-week high. Canada raised rates; the UK Budget passed calmly.

chapters.title: US Dollar
chapters.teaser: The Federal Reserve held rates, but two officials voted to hike now. Chair Kevin Warsh then sounded less urgent than feared, and the dollar index slipped from a two-week high to about 102.05. Markets still see a December hike as very likely.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Since the US–Iran war began in February, high oil has kept US inflation near 3.7%, and the Federal Reserve raised rates in September. Going into today, a hold was expected and a December hike was mostly priced, which had lifted the dollar to a two-week high. What changed: What was expected: a hold, with all the interest in any December signal. What happened at 1:00 PM CT: the Fed held its rate range at 3.75–4.00%, but Fed governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack voted for an immediate quarter-point hike, and the statement called growth "strong" rather than "solid". At the 1:30 PM press conference, Warsh said reaching stable prices does not hinge on any single date or data point, noted that credit has tightened and that market inflation expectations are moving the right way. He also said that from 2027 one meeting a year will be a strategy session with no rate vote. The dollar index fell from just above 102.4 to about 102.05, and the 2-year Treasury yield eased slightly; even so, futures priced a December hike at about 86%, up from about 78% on Tuesday. Earlier, the US goods trade deficit widened more than expected in September, with little market effect. What it means: The vote leaned hawkish but the chair did not. Two votes for a hike show pressure inside the Fed to act sooner, which keeps December very much alive and gives the dollar a floor. But Warsh refused to tie himself to December, so traders took some profit on the dollar's run into the meeting. The question to keep asking: does the next inflation reading make a December hike unavoidable?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: US third-quarter growth and the September PCE price index, the inflation measure the Fed watches most, both at 7:30 AM CT Thursday; core PCE is expected up 0.3% on the month. The next Fed decision is December 9.
numbers: Fed rate held at 3.75–4.00%; vote 10–2, two for a hike
December hike ~86% priced (CME FedWatch, from ~78% Tuesday)

scenarios.bear: Core PCE comes in soft or growth disappoints; with Warsh already sounding patient, December bets fade and the index slips toward 101.5.

chapters.title: Euro
chapters.teaser: The euro broke a five-day losing run, rising about 0.3% to near $1.116 as the dollar slipped after the Fed. German shoppers stayed gloomy. The European Central Bank decides on Thursday and is expected to hold.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: The euro has been weighed down by weak euro-area growth, France's budget troubles and costly energy imports, and had fallen five days in a row into today. The ECB is expected to hold this week and raise rates in December. What changed: Germany's GfK consumer mood index for November came in at −30.8, about as expected: households expect the economy to improve but still worry about prices and their income. The bigger move came from the US side: once Fed chair Kevin Warsh sounded less urgent about December, the dollar slipped and the euro rose about 0.3% to near $1.116, briefly near $1.117. What it means: Today's gain was about the dollar, not the euro area, so it rests on Thursday's US figures and the ECB. The ECB's job is to signal that a December hike is still coming without spooking French bond markets. The question to keep asking: can the ECB sound firm on inflation while France's debt stays under strain?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: euro-area economic sentiment at 5:00 AM CT Thursday, US growth and inflation figures at 7:30 AM CT, then the ECB decision at 8:15 AM CT and President Christine Lagarde's press conference at about 8:45 AM CT. Euro-area inflation and growth estimates follow Friday.

scenarios.bear: Lagarde sounds unsure about December, or French bond yields jump, or US inflation runs hot; the euro slips back below $1.112.

chapters.title: British Pound
chapters.teaser: Chancellor John Healey's first UK Budget passed calmly: borrowing is set to fall, and UK government bond yields edged lower. The pound dipped to $1.327 before the speech, then recovered to about $1.334 as the dollar weakened after the Fed.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: UK inflation is running well above target, so the Bank of England is all but certain to raise rates on November 5. The main near-term risk to the pound was that Healey's Budget would add a lot of borrowing and unsettle UK bonds. What changed: The Budget came in close to what bond markets wanted. The Office for Budget Responsibility cut its 2027 growth forecast to 1.0% from 1.6%, but borrowing is projected to fall from 4.2% of national income this year to 1.8% by 2030–31. The spare room against Healey's own borrowing rules shrank to £15 billion from £24 billion in March. The 10-year gilt yield fell slightly. The pound had touched a 12-day low near $1.327 before the speech and finished near $1.334 after the Fed. What it means: A calm Budget removes a risk without adding support: the pound now moves on the Bank of England and the dollar. Slower growth forecasts and thin spare room mean the Bank's hikes may not run long. The question to keep asking: after November, will the Bank of England hike again in December?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: UK money and credit figures Thursday, then the Bank of England decision on November 5 at 6:00 AM CT (US clocks change on November 1).

scenarios.base: Bank of England hike bets stay high; the pound holds between $1.328 and $1.340 into the November 5 decision.

scenarios.bear: UK bonds sell off after closer study of the Budget, or the dollar rebounds on hot US inflation; the pound slips below $1.328.

chapters.title: Japanese Yen
chapters.teaser: The dollar failed to hold above ¥158 after the Fed and ended near ¥157.8, slightly lower on the day. Tokyo inflation figures tonight and the Bank of Japan decision on Friday are next.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: The yen sits low because Japan's rates are far below those elsewhere and Japan imports costly energy. The Bank of Japan is expected to hold this week and hike in December, and Japan's finance minister has warned Tokyo is ready to step in to support the yen. What changed: The dollar rose to about ¥158.2 straight after the Fed decision, but Fed chair Kevin Warsh's patient tone pulled it back to near ¥157.8. There was no Japanese data today. What it means: The ¥158 area is acting as a ceiling: higher US rates push the dollar up against the yen, but the risk of Tokyo stepping in, plus a December Bank of Japan hike, holds it back. The question to keep asking: does Japanese inflation make a December hike look settled?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: Tokyo consumer prices for October at 6:30 PM CT tonight, US growth and inflation figures at 7:30 AM CT Thursday, then the Bank of Japan decision and new forecasts during Friday in Japan (Thursday night CT).

chapters.title: Swiss Franc
chapters.teaser: The franc was little changed near 0.830 per dollar. Swiss investor sentiment turned negative in October, but it was a survey, not a policy signal, and markets stayed calm.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Swiss inflation is near zero, so the Swiss National Bank holds rates at zero and has grown more relaxed about a weaker franc. The franc moves mostly on global fear rather than Swiss news. What changed: The UBS survey of investor expectations fell to −15.3 from +2.6, its sharpest drop since March, though views of current conditions improved. Calm markets after the Fed kept demand for the franc as a safe place for money low. What it means: With no rate move expected and calm markets, the franc has little to drive it. The question to keep asking: does anything frighten markets enough to send money into the franc?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: Swiss National Bank board member Petra Tschudin speaks Thursday, and the KOF economic barometer comes Friday. The next Swiss rate decision is December 10.

chapters.title: Australian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The Aussie rose to a five-week high near 70.6 US cents. Hotter-than-forecast Australian inflation made a Reserve Bank of Australia hike on November 3 likely, and a softer-sounding Fed helped too.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised rates four times this year to fight energy-driven inflation, while Australia's jobs market has weakened. What changed: Underlying inflation (the trimmed mean) rose 1.0% in the third quarter, as economists expected but above the bank's own 0.8% forecast; headline inflation for September was 4.3% a year. Governor Michele Bullock told lawmakers the board will debate next week whether four hikes are enough. Markets raised the odds of a November hike to about 80%. The Aussie gained after the figures, then again after the Fed, to about 70.6 cents. What it means: The Aussie now has one of the clearest rate-hike stories among the majors, which draws money in. Weak jobs remain the main reason the bank could still wait. The question to keep asking: does the bank deliver a fifth hike, and does it signal more?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: Australian import prices Thursday and producer prices Friday, then the Reserve Bank of Australia decision at 9:30 PM CT Monday, November 2.

scenarios.bull: A strong hike signal or a softer US dollar lifts it above 71 cents.
scenarios.bear: Hot US inflation lifts the dollar, or the bank hints it may wait; the Aussie slips below 70 cents.

chapters.title: Canadian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50%, its first hike since 2023, and said more may be needed. The loonie barely moved, closing near 1.4035 per US dollar, because the hike was mostly expected.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Energy and import costs have pushed Canadian inflation above the Bank of Canada's 1–3% range, even as US tariffs keep the economy soft. Hedge funds hold large bets against the loonie. What changed: The bank raised its rate by a quarter point to 2.50%, as most economists expected. Its new forecasts lift 2027 inflation to 3.1% from 2.0% and see inflation near 3.5% by the end of this year. Governor Tiff Macklem said a further increase could be needed but the bank will proceed carefully. Markets now give a December hike about a 45% chance, and Canada's 2-year yield hit a two-year high. The loonie gained only about 0.1%. What it means: The hike was in the price, so the loonie needed a bolder signal to rally. Rising Canadian yields and high oil give it support, but the cautious tone limits it. The question to keep asking: how fast is the Bank of Canada willing to go?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: Bank of Canada deputy governor Nicolas Vincent speaks at 9:50 AM CT Thursday, Canada's August GDP comes at 7:30 AM CT Friday, and the next decision is December 9.

scenarios.base: December stays a coin toss; the US dollar stays between 1.398 and 1.408 Canadian.
scenarios.bull: Firm comments from Vincent or strong Canadian GDP lift December hike bets; hedge funds buy back loonies and the US dollar falls below 1.398.
scenarios.bear: Oil drops or hot US inflation lifts the US dollar; it rises above 1.408 Canadian.

chapters.title: New Zealand Dollar
chapters.teaser: The kiwi stayed near 56 US cents after the Reserve Bank of New Zealand held rates at 2.75% when almost everyone expected a hike. The bank still says more tightening is likely, so December is open.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has been raising rates to bring down inflation, and markets were close to certain of another hike this week. What changed: The bank held at 2.75% in a 4–3 vote; 22 of 27 economists polled had expected a hike to 3.00%. The kiwi fell as much as 1.7%, to about 55.85 cents, and lost about 1.6% against the Aussie. All members agreed further tightening is likely. Blue Street has no verified kiwi level after the Fed. What it means: The hold reads as a delay, not a change of course, but it leaves the kiwi with a weaker rate story than the Aussie next door. The question to keep asking: does New Zealand's data make a December hike a sure thing again?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: New Zealand's ANZ business confidence survey for October on Thursday, then the next decision on December 9, with new forecasts.

chapters.title: Oil
chapters.teaser: Oil rose again, with Brent near $115.7 and US crude above $103, a one-week high. US crude stocks fell for a fourth week, and a report said the US told Gulf allies to brace for possible strikes on Iran after next week's US midterm elections.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Since the US–Iran war began in February, oil has carried a war premium. Talks involving Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials and Iran are under way, while Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia keep supply fears alive. What changed: Government figures showed US crude stocks fell 1.9 million barrels last week, against a small expected rise, though petrol stocks jumped. The Wall Street Journal reported the US warned Gulf allies to prepare for a short, intense campaign against Iran after the November 3 midterms; no decision has been made. Saudi Arabia has still not confirmed a Houthi claim of a hit on its biggest refinery, Ras Tanura. Brent was near $115.7 by late morning and US crude topped $103 in the afternoon. What it means: Supply risk is pushing up again as the hope from the talks fades. Higher oil helps exporters like Canada and Australia and costs importers like Japan and the euro area, and it keeps inflation pressure on central banks. The question to keep asking: do the talks with Iran lead anywhere before the US election?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: the OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, expected to keep December output targets unchanged, and the US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3.
numbers: US crude stocks −1.9M barrels (small rise expected)

scenarios.bear: Progress in the talks lets Brent fall below $112.

chapters.title: Gold
chapters.teaser: Gold slipped back toward $4,000 an ounce, from about $4,060 in the morning, as higher oil kept rate-hike fears alive. The Fed's hold and two votes for a hike gave it no lift.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Gold rallied this year on the US–Iran war and on fears for the dollar, then eased as central banks moved toward hikes, which make interest-paying assets more attractive than gold. What changed: Gold was near $4,060 early in the day. Rising oil revived worries about inflation and further hikes, and after the Fed's hold, with two officials voting to hike, gold resumed its slide toward $4,000. Blue Street has no verified closing price. What it means: Higher expected rates are weighing on gold more than the war is lifting it. A softer Fed tone did not change that. The question to keep asking: do US rate expectations keep rising?

calls.text: UK retail sales Fri 1:00 AM CT (−0.2% expected): a strong print lifts December hike bets and the pound; a weak one trims both
calls.note: Sales fell 0.4%, worse than expected, yet the pound reached its strongest against the euro since May 2025 on Friday as a November Bank of England hike stayed near certain.

calls.text: US jobless claims Thu 7:30 AM CT (about 200,000 expected): staying low keeps the Fed's December hike near 90%; a jump trims it and weighs on the dollar
calls.note: Claims stayed low at 194,000 (200,000 expected), near their lowest in decades. December hike bets held near 90% (CME FedWatch, Oct 21); a sharp bond rally later still pulled the dollar lower.

calls.text: Moody's review of France Fri: a downgrade widens France's gap over German yields and weighs on the euro; holding the rating eases the pressure
calls.note: Moody's held France at Aa3; French yields eased on Monday and the euro led the majors in the European morning.

calls.text: Bailey 8:00 AM CT after the 3.5% UK inflation print: backing November without promising more keeps the pound near $1.34; any opening to a December follow-up lifts it; calling energy temporary trims it
calls.note: Neither branch: Bailey gave no new signal on rates. The pound still held near $1.34 (about 1.3395 at the New York close), with December's second hike about a coin toss.

calls.text: US crude oil stocks 9:30 AM CT (industry survey: about −4.9M barrels): a big official draw keeps Brent above $110; a build lets the rebound fade
calls.note: The draw came (−3.1M barrels, far more than forecast) and Brent briefly topped $110.8, but it still faded to $108.82 at the settle after the US Treasury's tanker licence and emergency fuel loans.

calls.text: Pakistan's mediation after Iran's uranium refusal: any confirmed opening drains oil's premium and lifts the euro and yen; more warships and no talks keep Brent near $110 into the close
calls.note: No opening: Rubio called a deal extremely difficult and more US warships headed in. Brent settled at $108.82, near $110 but off its high on Washington's supply moves rather than diplomacy.

calls.text: Japan national CPI Thu 6:30 PM CT (2.1% expected): a hot print keeps the BoJ's December hike near three in four; a soft one fades it and weighs on the yen
calls.note: Neither branch: 2.1% exactly as expected (1.7% prior), though the measure that also leaves out energy jumped to 2.4%. December hike pricing held near 80%.

calls.text: US–Iran framework: confirmation by either government drains oil's risk premium and pulls US long yields lower; another denial puts Brent back toward $110
calls.note: No confirmation from either government, and no fresh denial either. Brent still climbed back toward $110 overnight, on tanker attacks spreading to the Gulf of Oman rather than on the talks.

calls.text: RBA's Hauser 5:30 PM CT: leaning on sticky inflation keeps a November hike near 1 in 3; leaning on the softer job market trims it
calls.note: Hauser leaned on sticky inflation: the outlook is 'materially worse'. Odds of a November hike rose to about 40% from about 30%, and the Aussie hit a three-week high near 0.702.

calls.text: China Q3 GDP 4.5% vs 4.4% fc — the aussie's demand read
calls.note: Beat: 4.5% vs 4.4% fc (q/q 1.2%); retail +1.1% the standout. AUD/USD +0.3-0.5% to ~0.697, the night's best G10 performer; USD/CNH 6.6811, strongest since June 2022. Two-speed beat (factories lead, property -20.6% YTD).

calls.text: Petersburg Oil Terminal drone strike — Baltic supply risk into Monday's open vs the waiver's lower-price pull
calls.note: Fire CONFIRMED (Beglov; Fire Point confirmed its FP-1 hit the terminal); ~1 killed, several injured (figures vary); damage extent still unquantified. Crude's Sunday open came flat — neither the spike nor the tumble; Asia Brent -1.0 to -1.8%.

calls.text: Beirut strike fallout: the haven-bid tell at Monday's open
calls.note: No Hezbollah retaliation as of Monday's open (Qmati: strike crossed a 'red line', leadership to decide; IDF: normal routines). Haven bid stayed sheathed — DXY flat 101.80-101.83, havens ~flat in Asia. The tell held: no escalation, no haven extension.

calls.text: October FOMC priced as a hold (~85%) into the Saturday blackout; December is the live debate
Brent broke $108 on Ukraine refinery strikes — $105-112 range into the weekend (prior $104-108 call broken)
USD/CAD holds 1.41-1.43 into the BoC (Oct 28); Canada CPI Mon the trigger
calls.note: Oct 19: CPI passed without a break — USD/CAD ~1.411 at the NY close, still inside the range. Runs to the Oct 28 decision. Oct 20: dipped to ~1.409, a hair under the floor, as oil and BoC hike bets lifted the loonie. Oct 20 close: broke below the floor — USD/CAD ~1.406, strongest loonie since Sep 22, on BoC hike pricing (~80–85%) and Alberta's vote to remain.
The tripwire never bit — Friday's waiver suspends the duties outright with no end date. Superseded by the ~Dec 17 60-day review clock.
calls.text: Graham Act Oct-18 tripwire: waivers extended or enforcement begins — oil's Sunday open is the tell
Iran deal Sunday signing: Trump's 'OPEN TO ALL' vs Tehran's 'not tomorrow' — the strait itself is the verdict
calls.note: No signed deal carried by any major wire by 4pm CT Sunday; Trump's 'complete' claim stands unverified against Tehran's 'talks stalled'. Aggregator 'markets celebrate' content held — its futures numbers contradict Friday's verified settles. The signing test is claim day, not done day.

calls.text: Canada CPI Mon 7:30am CT (TD 3.2%, UBS 3.3%, RBC 3.0%): hot (3.3%+) revives the Oct 28 hike; soft (3.0%-) buries it to December
calls.note: Neither branch: 3.1% vs 3.2% expected, core measures cooled to 1.8–1.9%. October stayed about 1 in 4 (a hold), with about one quarter-point hike priced by December; consumers' inflation expectations rose to ~3.9% in the BoC survey. Correction (Oct 20): by Monday's close swaps had jumped to ~87% for an October hike on Macklem's Saturday forecast warning; the 1-in-4 figure was stale.

calls.text: UK CPI Wed 1am CT (3.4% fc vs 3.1%): 3.5%+ starts pricing a December follow-up; soft reopens Bailey's 2027 read
calls.note: Hot branch: 3.5% vs 3.4% expected (3.1% in August), the highest in 11 months. November's hike is near certain; how much December moved was not yet verified at write.

calls.text: NZ Q3 CPI Wed 4:45pm CT (ANZ 3.8% y/y): hot settles the RBNZ's two-way bet toward the hike side
calls.note: Not hot: inflation came in at 3.7%, a touch soft. The hike side still settled anyway, with October 28 now about 98% priced.

calls.text: Japan CPI Fri + BoJ Oct 29-30: Ueda's 'quite close' language tested — October hike stays ~25%
calls.note: Oct 19: swaps now put an October 30 hike under 5% (BBH), below the ~25% in the call. December ~80% unchanged. October hike odds fell to about 4%, far below the ~25% in the call; Japan's inflation came in at 2.1% as expected and December (~80%) is now the meeting that matters.

calls.text: France's revenue-section budget vote Tue: a clean pass narrows the French–German spread (~141bp); a defeat or big concessions widens it and weighs on the euro
calls.note: No vote on Tuesday: it was pushed to October 27, so neither branch played out.

calls.text: UK jobs Tue 1 AM CT (earnings ~3.8% expected): sticky pay firms the BoE hike case before Wednesday's inflation; cooling pay backs Bailey's calmer view
calls.note: Sticky side won: unemployment fell to 4.7% (4.9% expected) and regular pay rose 3.7% (3.6% expected); total pay and claims were softer. Pound +0.3% to ~1.334.

calls.text: Konarak follow-through: a US confirmation or more strikes keeps oil's supply premium and lifts US yields; silence lets the morning's waiver drop resume
calls.note: No confirmation (a US official denied the strike) and no new strike overnight, yet the premium held: Brent ~$109.8 Tuesday on low Gulf flows and Iran's Hormuz claims. The waiver-driven drop did not resume.

calls.text: BoC Oct 28 with ~87% priced for a hike: a hike is mostly in the loonie already; a hold would be the surprise and hit it
NZ Q3 CPI Wed 4:45pm CT (~3.8% y/y): near forecast keeps the ~80% hike pricing; clearly soft reopens the hold and weighs on the kiwi
calls.note: Near forecast (3.7% vs 3.8%) and hike pricing held, rising to about 98%; the kiwi dipped only briefly.
